5451.loc: p. 120, Lautlehre Kap. I par. 1-2 'Tonhoehen' (par. 3 continues on p. 121)
5451.idn: Name in the source: /Xam-Buschmännisch (Dialekt der /xam-Buschmänner); family in the source: Buschmannsprachen (Bushman); in D. Bleek's quoted remark 'Südbuschmännisch' (Southern Bushman), contrasted with Nordbuschmännisch (!Kung)

tn.quote: § 1. Buschmännisch gehört zu den „Tonhöhensprachen“, d. h. Sprachen, welche sonst völlig gleiche Wörter in verschiedenen Bedeutungen durch verschiedene Tonhöhen bzw. -bewegungen unterscheiden. Über Tonhöhen im Buschm. erfahren wir aus unseren Texten wenig. … wozu D. Bl. brieflich folgendes bemerkt: „Südbuschmännisch, wie z. B. die /χam-Sprache, hat im Vergleich wenige hohe und tiefe Töne. …“ § 2. Nach D. Bleeks brieflichen Mitteilungen wäre allerdings für den Tiefton ein häufiges Zeichen in der Gestalt eines Hakens, unter dem Vokal gebraucht
tn.translation: Par. 1. Bushman belongs to the 'pitch (tone) languages', i.e. languages which distinguish otherwise wholly identical words of different meanings by different pitches or pitch movements. ... About pitches in Bushman we learn little from our texts. ... D. Bl[eek] remarks by letter as follows: 'Southern Bushman, e.g. the /Xam language, has comparatively few high and low tones. Northern Bushman, such as !Kung, has many more.' ... Par. 2. According to D. Bleek's communications by letter, however, a frequent sign for the low tone, in the shape of a hook under the vowel, is used
tn.cite: Meriggi, Piero. 1928/29. Versuch einer Grammatik des /Xam-Buschmännischen. Zeitschrift für Eingeborenen-Sprachen 19: 117-153, 188-205. Berlin: D. Reimer.
tn.locator: p. 120, Lautlehre Kap. I par. 1-2 'Tonhoehen' (par. 3 continues on p. 121)
tn.note: Called a tone language; texts mark a raised (high) tone and, per D. Bleek, a low tone (hook); /Xam said to have few high and low tones; grave/acute on some pronouns read as low/high; no count given. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): quotation re-keyed from the source (p. 120, Lautlehre Kap. I §§ 1-2 'Tonhöhen').

corr.words: § 1. Buschmännisch gehört zu den „Tonhöhensprachen“, … „Südbuschmännisch, wie z. B. die /χam-Sprache, hat im Vergleich wenige hohe und tiefe Töne. …“ § 2. Nach D. Bleeks brieflichen Mitteilungen wäre allerdings für den Tiefton ein häufiges Zeichen in der Gestalt eines Hakens, unter dem Vokal gebraucht

5452.idn: Name in the source: XZ Lalo (Xuzhang Lalo; also 'Xuzhang Lalu'); family in the source: Lalo < Central Ngwi < Ngwi (Loloish) < Burmic (Lolo-Burmese) < Tibeto-Burman (Bradley 2002b)

tn.quote: XZ Lalo shares the same syllable template as YL: (C)V(N)T, in which the optional initial is one of 30 consonants, an obligatory vowel (one of 13 vowels or 1 syllabic fricative), an optional nasal final /-,/, and tone (one of 4). All tones are in modal phonation. … Unlike any other Lalo variety, XZ has merged *3, *H, *L to the mid level tone [33]. The resulting system contrasts four tones: High, Mid, Low, and Low-rising, as seen in Table 3-46 below. … The Tone *1 split and merger of *3, *H and *L leaves XZ with three equally spaced level tones and one rising tone.
tn.cite: Yang, Cathryn. 2010. Lalo regional varieties: phylogeny, dialectometry, and sociolinguistics. PhD thesis, Linguistics Program, La Trobe University, Bundoora, Victoria. doi:10.26181/21844209.v1

tn.note: Four tones on every (C)V(N) syllable, all modal voice: high 55 (often [453] in isolation), mid 33, low 21 and low-rising 24; three level tones and one rising; F0 plots of one speaker.

5454.idn: Name in the source: Yintale (also Yintalaing, Yantalaing; Shan 'Yangtalai'; Kayah 'Tah-liah'); family in the source: Karen (Karenic) languages, Sino-Tibetan; 'a south-western group of Kayah' (Bradley 1997 cited)

tn.quote: According to this data, all tones are in contrast. There are five contrastive tones in Yintale. Each tone is referred to by demonstrating diacritics. They are high //, mid //, low //, falling // and rising //. … According to this data, there are five phonemic tones in Yintale: high, falling, mid, low and rising. … With five tones and three syllable words, the number of possible patterns is 125, but only twenty-six patterns are seen in this data. Rising and falling tones tend to occur only on the third syllable, sequences of HH-X and HM-X are common as are LH-X and LL-X.
tn.cite: Myar Doo Myar Reh. 2004. A phonological comparison of selected Karenic language varieties of Kayah State. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xix+180 pp.

tn.note: Five contrastive tones: high, mid, low, falling and rising, one on each syllable; in three-syllable words falling and rising tend to occur only on the last syllable. Silent on word stress.

tn.quote: Zaachila Zapotec and San Lucas Quiaviní Zapotec have the same interaction patterns between the four contrastive phonation types and the four tones. … Table 7. Zaachila Zapotec tone and voice combinations ZAACHILA ZAPOTEC H L F R … in San Lucas Quiaviní Zapotec and Zaachila Zapotec only low and falling tones can co-occur with all the contrastive phonation types. … In both languages rising tone does not co-occur with non-modal vowels. refs.ref: Apia, N’Guessan Edmond. 2025. L’abbey: à l’épreuve d’un alphabet et d’une orthographe stables. Djiboul, Revue des Arts-Communication, Lettres, Sciences Humaines et Sociales, N°009, Vol. 3 (juillet 2025), pp. 240-251. Abidjan: Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny.

5456.idn: Name in the source: abbey; family in the source: langue kwa de Côte d’Ivoire (Kwa)

tn.quote: L’abbey est une langue à tons. On y rencontre deux types de tons lexicaux: les tons ponctuels et les tons modulés. Les tons ponctuels sont au nombre de trois; ce sont: les tons haut, moyen et bas, représentés, respectivement, par les symboles (ˊ), ( ̄ ) et (ˋ). … Quant au ton moyen, il ne se rencontre qu’en position médiane et en position finale. … Les tons modulés, quant à eux, sont au nombre de deux; ce sont: les tons modulés descendant et montant. … Tous les tons sont marqués au-dessus des noyaux de syllabes que sont les voyelles. Exemples: cá [cá] « Epoux »; jā [jā] « Epouse » …
tn.translation: Abbey is a tone language. Two types of lexical tones occur: level tones and contour tones. The level tones are three: high, mid and low, written (ˊ), (̄) and (ˋ). … The mid tone occurs only in medial and final position. … The contour tones are two: falling and rising. … All tones are marked above the syllable nuclei, i.e. the vowels. Examples: cá 'husband'; jā 'wife' …
tn.cite: Apia, N’Guessan Edmond. 2025. L’abbey: à l’épreuve d’un alphabet et d’une orthographe stables. Djiboul, Revue des Arts-Communication, Lettres, Sciences Humaines et Sociales, N°009, Vol. 3 (juillet 2025), pp. 240-251. Abidjan: Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny.
tn.note: Tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low) and two contour tones (falling, rising), marked on every syllable nucleus; mid tone never word-initial except in numerals; nothing on stress.

5456.cfw: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

5460.idn: Name in the source: Bekwarra; family in the source: classed (as 'Yakoro') with Boki and Gayi (Uge) as 'Cross River 1', part of the larger Benue-Congo grouping, by Greenberg (1963)

tn.quote: The basic tone-bearing unit is the syllabic, syllables (with a few special exceptions) being of the pattern CV (consonant - vowel), V (vowel) or N (syllabic nasal). Each of these normally bears a single unit of tone, viz. high, mid or low (abbreviated H, M and L respectively). … When the tone associated with a non-word-initial V or N syllable differs from that of a preceding syllable (which must be of structure CV) the two tones together are realised as a rising or falling pitch extending over the two syllables …
tn.cite: Stanford, Ronald. 1967. The Bekwarra language of Nigeria: a grammatical description. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London. 326 pp.
tn.locator: thesis p. 31, ch. 2 section 2.2.1 'General' (under 2.2 Tone)
tn.note: Three level tones, high, mid and low, one on each syllable (CV, V or syllabic nasal); rising and falling glides analysed as sequences of two level tones; verbs fall into H, M and L tone classes.

5461.idn: Name in the source: Bhele; family in the source: Bantu (Grammar page: noun class system 'typical of many Bantu languages', 'related Bantu languages')

tn.quote: Bhele has two tone registers, High and Low. All four pa erns of High and Low are a ested on disyllabic noun roots. Contour tones can be seen as a combina on of a Low and a High tone, linked to the same syllable. … Verb roots have either a High tone or a Low tone, linked to the ﬁrst syllable of the root. … Some disyllabic High nouns are realized with a High tone on the ﬁrst syllable and a lower tone (but not at the level Low) on the second. As yet it is unknown whether this is another tone level, or (non)automa c downstep. … Bhele has gramma cal tone …
tn.cite: Raymond, Timothy R. & Gerrit de Wit. 2025. Notes on Bhele phonology ('Phonology page', final v3, dated June 2025). In: Bhele Dictionary (Bhele - French - Swahili - English), Webonary.org. SIL Global.

tn.quote: Dana displays three contrastive tone levels (L, M, H) as well as a falling (F) contour tone on a single vowel nucleus. Evidence for the tonal contrast is seen in (31). (31) H M L F d̪ ám d̪ ā d̪ à d̪ â ‘thing’ ‘go.SG’ ‘what’ ‘go.PL’ … Tone plays an important role in the verb system. Dana employs tonal alternations on verb roots and stems to mark nominal number of participants as well as verbal number, or pluractionality (cf. Newman 1990). … Most common is the alternation between L and H. The M/H and F/LH alternations are less frequent in the database overall.

5465.idn: Name in the source: Chen; family in the source: Sino-Tibetan > Tibeto-Burman > Sal > Northern Naga > Konyak

tn.quote: Chen exhibits four tones, three of which are level tones and one falling. Phonation plays a role in the tone system: three tones are produced with modal phonation and one with glottalisation. … Open syllables may carry any of the four tones, syllables that end in a nasal may carry tone 1, 2, or 3, and syllables that end in a stop have the least options - they may carry only tone 2 or 3. … tone 1 has a mid to low falling contour. … Tone 4, as indicated in Table 8, is characterised by a high level pitch contour and glottalisation.
tn.cite: Konyak, Hoipo & Mijke Mulder. 2022. A brief outline of Chen phonology [Thai parallel title: โครงสร้างฉบับร่างของสัทวิทยาภาษาเฉิน]. In: Proceedings of the Payap University and UNRN Research Symposium 2022 (รายงานสืบเนื่องจากการประชุมวิชาการฯ พ.ศ. 2565), Chiang Mai, 11 February 2022, linguistics section, pp. 709-721. Chiang Mai: Payap University, Research and Academic Service Office.
tn.locator: sec. 4 'Suprasegmental phonology: the tone system', pp. 716-717 with Table 8 'Chen tones'
tn.note: Four tones: tone 1 mid-to-low falling (31), tone 2 high (55), tone 3 low (11), tone 4 high (55) with glottalisation; stop-final syllables take only tones 2-3; minor syllables carry no tone.

5466.loc: pp. 313-314, sections 'Tone' and 'Downdrift and downstep with Plateauing'
5466.idn: Name in the source: Cicipu; family in the source: Kambari subgroup (not Kamuku) of Kainji (Benue-Congo)

tn.quote: Cicipu vowels are found with two contrastive tones: H and L, with contour tones being found on long vowels and diphthongs. … Verb lexemes are inherently toneless, deriving their surface tones from their Tense-Aspect- Mood properties … Falling or rising tones can occur phonetically as a consequence of applying a particular tone pattern to a long vowel, diphthong, or sequence of two vowels. … Note that while LH tones can arise from the overlay of grammatical tone patterns, they are never lexically specified. … Non-automatic downstepped H tones also occur.
tn.cite: McGill, Stuart. 2014. Cicipu. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 44(3): 303-318 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S002510031400022X
tn.locator: pp. 313-314, sections 'Tone' and 'Downdrift and downstep with Plateauing'
tn.note: Two level tones, H and L; contours only on long vowels or diphthongs, as tone sequences. Nouns have lexical root tone, verbs are toneless and take mood/aspect melodies; non-automatic downstep.

tn.quote: Basically there are two discrete tone levels, high and low, together with a feature of downstep, lowering of the high tone level (3.14). Tone signals lexical contrasts … and also has direct semantic relevance in that it realizes features of tense and polarity in the structure of the Verbal Group (3.5) … gliding tones occur only on the final syllable of the word-piece. … Underlying tones on all non-final syllables in the word-piece are simple, being either high or low. Underlying tones on all final syllables are complex, being a combination of two tones

PhD thesis, University of London (Department of General Linguistics, University College London). 314 pp. ProQuest no. 10673257; SOAS Research Online copy, DOI 10.25501/soas.00029013.

tn.note: Two level tones, high and low, with distinctive (non-automatic) downstep of high, partly from latent low tones; falling/rising glides only word-finally, analysed as HL/LH; tone marks tense/polarity.

5468.loc: p. 98, section 2.3 'Loan phonology', with table 2 'Influence in phonology'
5468.idn: Name in the source: Htanaw; family in the source: Austroasiatic; a primary branch of the Palaungic group

tn.quote: One of the most intriguing features of Htanaw phonology is the presence of three lexical tones (four according to some authors). On the surface, this looks similar to the Burmese tone system … The phonetic realization of the tones are not identical in the two languages … Tones in Htanaw do not only have lexical function, but they also express grammatical functions. Most prominently, in possessive and oblique contexts, low and mid tones change to high. … Table 2: Influence in phonology … Tones Low-falling, Mid-falling, … High-rising … Gramm. tone L, M → H; POSS, OBL
tn.cite: Jenny, Mathias, Han Tin, Rachel Weymuth & Alexandra Herdeg. 2025. Burmese as a linguistic resource for Htanaw. In Paul Sidwell (ed.), Austroasiatic Linguistics in honour of Michel Ferlus (1935-2024), 93-105. Chiang Mai: Myanmar Center, Faculty of Humanities, Chiang Mai University.

tn.note: Three lexical tones: low-falling, mid-falling, high-rising (also called low, mid, high; four according to some authors); low and mid become high in possessive/oblique forms of some kin terms.

5469.loc: pp. 122-123, sec. 1 Introduction, ex. (2) on p. 123
5469.idn: Name in the source: Nyala-East; family in the source: a variety of the Luyia (aka 'Luhya') macrolanguage [luy]; Bantu

tn.quote: In all Luyia languages, verb inflection is characterized by distinctive ‘ melodic H’ (H M) tones on specific positions of the (macro) stem. … Reversive languages, like Bukusu and Nyala‑East, are geographically and, we hypothesize, historically intermediate between conservative and predictable varieties. Forms in (2) show that, like conservative languages, reversive systems retain a two‑way tone distinction in verb roots, but like predictable languages, all verbs have a H M . (2) Nyala‑East (reversive) * Ø verbs a‑lá[ kúlíx‑á] ‘ he will name’ * H verbs a‑lá[ xalák‑á] ‘ he will cut’
tn.cite: Ebarb, Kristopher J., Christopher R. Green & Michael R. Marlo. 2014. Luyia tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 121-143.
tn.locator: pp. 122-123, sec. 1 Introduction, ex. (2) on p. 123
tn.note: Bantu (Luyia) tone system of the 'reversive' type: verb roots keep a two-way lexical contrast (toneless vs. high) and every verb form also carries an inflectional melodic high tone.

5470.loc: thesis pp. 30-31 (continues to p. 32), ch. 2 'The Transcription', sec. 2.4 'Tone'
5470.idn: Name in the source: Ekpeye; family in the source: closely related to Igbo but not mutually intelligible with it; 'must be recognised as a separate language' (neighbours Ogba and Ikwere 'also related to Igbo')

tn.quote: The tone-bearing unitw is the syllable, which is of the pattern V, OV, or rarely N. There are five units of tone, three of level pitch, and two of gliding pitch* The three level tones are termed High, Low and Downstep … "Doivnstep” is used as a label rather than "Mid" since this tone occurs only after a high* After a Low, the contrast between High and Downstep is neutralised* … The two gliding tones both show a fall in pitch, one from High to Low, the other from High to Downstep* … Very few tonal minimal pairs have been found. Thus, lexically tone carries a low functional load
tn.cite: Clark, David John. 1969. A grammatical study of Ekpeye. PhD thesis, School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. 327 pp.
tn.locator: thesis pp. 30-31 (continues to p. 32), ch. 2 'The Transcription', sec. 2.4 'Tone'
tn.note: Five tones on the syllable: level High, Low and Downstep (Downstep only after a High), plus High-to-Low and High-to-Downstep falling glides; downdrift over the sentence; few lexical minimal pairs.

5471.loc: p. 386, sec. 1 'Introduction' (opening paragraphs) and p. 387, sec. 1.2 'Tonal contours'
5471.idn: Name in the source: Kifuliiru; family in the source: Bantu J (Interlacustrine) language of the Shi-Havu cluster

tn.quote: Verb roots in Kifuliiru fall into three classes: High (H), Low (L) and toneless (Ø). The lexical tone (if any) of the verb always appears in stem‑initial position. … Verbal extensions are all toneless with the exception of Passive (PS), Causative (CS), and CS + PS, any of which contributes a single floating H tone. Every Tense/ Aspect/ Mood (TAM) includes one of six melodies: H, L, HL, LH, HH or LL. … Tonal contours in Kifuliiru appear exclusively in the penult … Therefore I posit that tone association is to the syllable, not to the mora.
tn.cite: Van Otterloo, Karen. 2014. Tonal melodies in the Kifuliiru verbal system. Africana Linguistica 20: 385-403. doi:10.3406/aflin.2014.1041
tn.locator: p. 386, sec. 1 'Introduction' (opening paragraphs) and p. 387, sec. 1.2 'Tonal contours'
tn.note: Two tones, H and L (toneless units surface L by default); verb roots are H, L or toneless; each tense adds one of six H/L melodies; HL/LH contours only on the penult; syllable TBU; floating H.

5472.idn: Name in the source: Guébie; family in the source: Kru; 'an Eastern Kru language' (p. 419)

tn.quote: Guébie has four contrastive tone heights labelled 1–4, of which 4 is the highest. All morphemes, with the exception of the definite suffix (Sande 2017), are associated with an underlying tone melody, and surface with that tone melody unless some phonological or grammatical tonal alternation applies. … a super­high tone, tone 5, can also surface. A tone 5 is derived from an underlying high tone, tone 4, plus a grammatical tone raising process. Contrastive underlying tone melodies include levels 1, 2, 3 and 4 and contours 41, 42, 31, 32, 23 and 24.
tn.cite: Sande, Hannah. 2022. Is grammatical tone item-based or process-based? Phonology 39(3): 399-442. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0952675723000106 (first published online 2 October 2023; CC BY 4.0).
tn.locator: p. 409 sec. 2.2 and p. 419 sec. 3.2
tn.note: Four contrastive tone heights (1 low to 4 high); every morpheme carries an underlying melody, a level or a two-height contour (41 42 31 32 23 24), mapped left to right; floating high marks negation.

tn.quote: 14% There are three basic tones in Gwari: low (a), mid (a) and high (4)- Honosyllabic verb stems bear one of these three tones. … In addition, a fourth level tone slightly lower than mid, as well as a rising tone (8) and a falling tone (4) are found. … After a low tone syllable, mid tone becomes lower-mid, while high tone becomes rising tone- A second low tone remains low. … 18. A lower-mid tone is in most cases a mid tone that has been slightly lowered as the result of a preceding low tone- Very often that low tone no longer occurs phonetically, but still exerts its lowering effect.

5474.idn: Name in the source: Gera; family in the source: West Chadic language, Afro-Asiatic language family (Chadic)

tn.quote: Gera is also tonal language just like Hausa. Gera has two types of tones; high and low tones. But the different is that unlike Hausa, tone in Gera is only used in one category that is to distinguish between lexical items. Example: Wula (L,L) (goats) Wula (H,L) (rope) Ewi (H,L) snake Ewi ((L,L) fear Lumba (H,L) (hundred) Lumba (L,H) (leaf for draw soap) … Lumba (L,L) (follow) Rini (L,H) (today) Rini (H,H) (Shadow) Waya (HH) (Medicine) Waya(HL) (Smoke
